entries.author: carol
entries.body: Decide the authentication approach for the public API and the admin dashboard before beta.

entries.author: carol
entries.body: We need one decision that operations can actually support in the first release.

entries.author: carol
entries.body: External OIDC providers give us mature MFA, recovery, and federation flows that are expensive to reproduce internally.

entries.author: bob
entries.body: The public API already has a browser SPA client and the mobile app will need token-based access soon.

entries.author: dave
entries.body: We do not have a low-latency shared session store across regions in the current platform.

entries.author: alice
entries.body: We should prefer an approach that lets us revoke compromised access quickly during incident response.

entries.author: bob
entries.body: Use self-issued JWT access tokens for both the public API and the admin dashboard.

entries.author: alice
entries.body: Use HTTP-only session cookies backed by our application for both the admin dashboard and browser clients.

entries.author: carol
entries.body: Use a third-party OIDC provider for all authentication and rely on its hosted flows.

entries.author: alice
entries.body: Self-issued JWTs are hard to revoke before expiry unless we also run a denylist or token introspection service.

entries.author: alice
entries.body: If disabled users keep valid tokens for too long, the security team loses a practical way to contain account compromise.

entries.author: alice
entries.body: I could only support self-issued JWTs if we also commit to near-immediate revocation for disabled or compromised accounts.

entries.author: dave
entries.body: The admin dashboard is used only by employees in browsers, so cookie-based UX is acceptable there.

entries.author: carol
entries.body: Regional failover becomes risky if the session store turns into an implicit control plane dependency.

entries.author: bob
entries.body: A third-party identity provider adds vendor cost, tenant setup overhead, and a migration burden for the team.

entries.author: carol
entries.body: Splitting workforce auth from public API auth may resolve the apparent tradeoff instead of forcing one mechanism everywhere.

entries.author: carol
entries.body: Use an external OIDC provider for workforce and admin auth, issue provider-backed JWTs for the public API, and keep a thin adapter layer so we can swap vendors later.

entries.author: carol
entries.body: A narrow identity adapter keeps provider-specific code out of the application so a later migration stays feasible.

entries.author: dave
entries.body: A provider outage could lock administrators out during an incident unless we preserve a documented break-glass path.

entries.author: dave
entries.body: I like the direction, but I need a concrete outage story before I can consent.

entries.author: alice
entries.body: If we keep two audited local break-glass admin accounts outside the provider, the outage risk becomes operationally acceptable.

entries.author: bob
entries.body: This preserves mobile-friendly tokens without asking us to invent our own authentication stack from scratch.

entries.author: carol
entries.body: Decision: move forward with the hybrid plan, document vendor exit constraints, and track break-glass controls in the rollout checklist.
